## A Tale of Two Animated Films: Hexed and Wildwood

The release of Disney's animated feature **Hexed** has arrived, and for many, it’s conjured a curious sense of déjà vu, particularly for those who followed the journey of **Wildwood**. While **Hexed** aimed to explore a magical realm, its own behind-the-scenes narrative reads like a chapter ripped from the book of creative upheaval. The film, initially announced at D23 in August 2025 as a story about a teenage boy and his mother entering a world of magic, underwent a significant gender swap for its protagonist by CinemaCon in April 2026, just seven months before its release.

This last-minute pivot from a male lead, Billy, to a female lead, Billie (voiced by **Hailee Steinfeld**), has fueled speculation. As the Reactor Mag review suggests, the reasons behind this change are murky, with speculation ranging from executive concerns about the character seeming "too gay" to a desire to preemptively counter potential "anti-male" criticisms of a story where a son might accept his mother as the primary hero. Regardless of the true motive, such drastic shifts so late in production often signal a troubled creative path, a sentiment that resonates with the complex production history that also surrounded **Wildwood**.

## Echoes of Grief and Ambition in Animated Worlds

**Wildwood**, itself a 2026 release, captivated audiences with its PG-13 rating and a story about a headstrong teenager navigating a perilous forest to rescue her kidnapped brother. The film delves into themes of grief and ambition, populated by talking animals and powerful figures. The review for **Hexed** notes the inclusion of a "full-on unforgivable villain" named Celeste, a departure from the more morally ambiguous characters often found in similar thematic formulas. This villain's presence, coupled with the observation that "some people are just mean," as stated by the feline familiar Beef Roger Crummchuk (voiced by **Walton Goggins**), offers a stark contrast to the nuanced characterizations that might be expected. It’s a point that resonates in a world grappling with complex societal issues, suggesting a desire to present clearer moral lines, even within fantastical narratives.

The comparison between **Hexed** and **Wildwood** isn't just about release dates; it's about the shared DNA of ambitious animated projects facing significant creative hurdles. Both films, despite their different narrative focuses, seem to grapple with the challenges of translating complex themes and characters to the screen, often under the intense pressure of major studio expectations. The turbulent development of **Hexed** raises questions about the compromises made and whether the final product truly reflects the initial creative vision, a concern that often shadows ambitious animated features.

## What's Next

As **Hexed** settles into its release, audiences will continue to dissect its narrative and creative choices. The discourse surrounding its production, particularly in comparison to other ambitious animated films like **Wildwood**, will likely continue to unfold. Further details regarding the original intentions behind **Hexed** may emerge as more insights into its development process become public.

By Reuben Baron | Published on November 24, 2026 Credit: Disney Comment 0 Share New Share Hexed Just Made Me Want to Watch Wildwood Again&url= target=”_blank” title=”Twitter”> Hexed Just Made Me Want to Watch Wildwood Again” target=”_blank” title=”Pinterest”> Credit: Disney My curiosity about Hexed has mostly been about wanting to know what exactly happened behind the scenes here. The movie was first announced in August 2025 at D23 as a movie about “an awkward teenage boy” and his mom entering a world of magic. By CinemaCon in April 2026 (just seven months before its November release), the previously announced directors had already changed (Fawn Veerasunthorn joined while Josie Trinidad got demoted to co-director; Jason Hand’s directing credit stayed consistent between versions) and suddenly the boy lead was now a girl. As of this writing, the story hasn’t come out about why Billy became Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) at the last minute. My instinct, knowing how Disney has operated in recent years, was to assume executives thought the boy version of this character came off too gay (probably in some coded abstract sense; as with most of Disney’s post- Frozen features, Hexed has nary a hint of any romance). After seeing the movie, I wonder if it was even stupider than that: Maybe they thought an ending where a son accepts his mom being the big “chosen one” hero over himself would get attacked as “anti-male” by culture warriors and turning the son into a daughter was the safest way to avoid that. If it sounds too stupid to even imagine a major movie studio making creative decisions based on fearing reactions from that crowd, remember these three words: Rise of Skywalker . Listening to the internet is the root of too many bad decisions in Hollywood. The internet has, of course, had other blow-ups of discourse surrounding Hexed . I’m not going to recount every strange controversy about the film, but one that’s worth addressing is the fear that Hexed was ripping off The Owl House . The Owl House was a great cartoon that got cut short by Disney Channel (likely because of its LGBTQ+ representation), so I get why seeing Disney selling another animated project about a quirky girl transported to another world where she learns magic rubbed some Owl House fans the wrong way. Having seen the film, however, I can assure you that beyond those obvious parallels of witch-centric portal fantasy (and Owl House lead actress Sarah-Nicole Robles having a minor role here), the two stories have nothing in common. Hexed is NOT a rip-off of The Owl House . Which isn’t to say Hexed is original. It’s not—like, at all.
